        Measure
        1
        Only what we need to begin
        The few details that actually shape the course — what it is called, where it lives, how long it runs and roughly how many topics. The number of topics feeds straight into the outline we build later. Everything else Moodle asks for today is still there, just not here: it can wait until the course exists.
        2
        What students should be able to do
        Outcomes come first, in the teacher’s own words — no jargon, no verb picker. Everything built afterwards can be checked against them, which is the whole point of constructive alignment. How many a course needs, and whether that number is a requirement or a recommendation, are decided by the site.
        3
        Optional help writing them
        A teacher facing a blank box can ask for a first draft, then keep, edit or throw away each suggestion — nothing is added until they say so. Here it works from the course name alone to keep the demo simple; a real version would use more of what the teacher has already told us. Entirely optional: the course can be built without it.
        4
        How should students spend their time?
        These six are ABC Learning Design, a well-established way of describing what learners do — read, investigate, practise, discuss, work together, produce. Moodle Academy has used it since 2021. Asking now, rather than later, is what lets us suggest a sensible first outline instead of handing over an empty course.
        5
        A way through for everyone
        Not every teacher wants a framework, and nobody should have to argue with one to make a course. Skip is on the same screen as the other options, never hidden behind “more”, and it leads to an ordinary empty course with the normal Add activity button. The pedagogical route is the default, not a toll gate.
        6
        A preview of the course itself
        This is the course page, shown before the course exists, so teachers can shape the real thing rather than a summary of it. Two changes for this context: nothing claims a status the course cannot have yet, and every card and topic explains why it was suggested — so the teacher can disagree with the reasoning, not just the result.
        7
        What actually stops you
        Only the handful of things Moodle genuinely cannot create a course without. Everything else is a note, not a barrier — you can create the course and come back. Sites that want the outcome minimum enforced can switch it to a requirement; the State panel shows both.
        8
        Created now, finished later
        The course and every activity in it exist already. What is not finished is hidden from students until it is — so a teacher can build the whole shape in one sitting and fill in the content over the following week, without anyone seeing a half-built course.
        9
        Placeholders that say what they need
        This activity was created for you, but it cannot do its job yet — a page with no content, a quiz with no questions. The card says exactly what is missing and takes you straight to the form that asks for it. Until then it stays hidden, so students never meet an empty activity.
        10
        The thinking is kept, not thrown away
        Each activity remembers the kind of learning it was chosen for, and a teacher can change it. That is what the Alignment report reads to show the balance of the course. Only teachers see it; to students it is just the activity.
        11
        Prototype controls
        Not part of the design. Switches between the create flow and the finished course, between the outcome minimum being required or recommended, and between the two ways of shaping the outline.
